questions.q: What is the fundamental difference between distillation and quantization/pruning?
options: Distillation trains a new, usually differently-shaped student model; quantization and pruning compress an existing model's weights in place
Distillation only works on CPUs, while quantization and pruning only work on GPUs
Distillation removes weights, while quantization and pruning change the architecture
There is no real difference between them
questions.explain: Distillation trains a brand-new student model, often with a genuinely different (smaller) architecture, while quantization and pruning both start from the existing trained model and compress it directly.

questions.q: Why does distillation train the student on the teacher's 'soft targets' rather than only the ground-truth label?
options: Soft targets are faster to compute than ground-truth labels
The teacher's full probability distribution encodes richer information, such as which wrong answers were close, than a single correct label can
Ground-truth labels are never available in a distillation setup
Soft targets eliminate the need for a loss function entirely
questions.explain: A teacher's full output distribution over the vocabulary carries more signal than one correct answer — it implicitly shows which incorrect options were nearly right, which the student can learn from.

questions.q: What does the temperature parameter do in the distillation loss?
options: It increases the student model's physical GPU temperature
It flattens the teacher's (and student's) probability distribution so near-zero probabilities carry more learnable signal
It removes the need for cross-entropy loss entirely
It controls how many layers the student model has
questions.explain: Raw softmax output is often sharply peaked, hiding useful signal. Temperature spreads probability mass across more tokens before the loss is computed, making relative confidence easier to learn from.

questions.q: Why is distillation generally more expensive than quantization or pruning?
options: It requires a real training run (and often a sizable dataset), unlike the calibration pass GPTQ or AWQ use, or a magnitude-based pruning decision
Distillation requires no GPU at all, which makes it slower on CPU
It is actually cheaper than quantization in every case
Distillation can only be done by the original model's creators
questions.explain: Distillation is a genuine training run requiring GPU time and typically a meaningful dataset — much closer in cost to fine-tuning than to the minutes-to-hours calibration pass used by PTQ methods.

questions.q: Can a distilled student model also be quantized or pruned afterward?
options: No, distillation and quantization/pruning are mutually exclusive
Only pruning can be applied after distillation, never quantization
Yes — a distilled student is a normal model afterward, so quantization and pruning can be applied on top of it
Only if the student model is retrained from scratch first
questions.explain: The three compression levers stack rather than substitute for each other: a distilled student model can be further compressed with quantization and/or pruning for deployment.
